title: Find the power of a number (e.g., 2^10) using recursion (`power(x,n) = x * power(x, n-1)`, base: `power(x,0) = 1`).
shortTitle: Find the Power of a Number Using Recursion

s1_definition.profdef: Raising a number x to an integer power n means multiplying x by itself n times. Recursively, the power of x to the n equals x multiplied by the power of x to the n minus one, with the base case that any number to the power zero is one. This naive recursion makes n calls and runs in linear time, while the fast-exponentiation variant that squares the result of the half power runs in logarithmic time by halving the exponent each step.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India computes how Rajesh's fixed deposit grows when a fixed growth factor is applied every year for several years. Applying the factor for five years is the factor multiplied by itself five times. The recursive idea is simple: growth over five years equals the factor times the growth over four years, and growth over zero years is just one, meaning no growth applied yet. Each step peels off one year until there are none left.
s1_definition.oneliner: Power of x to n is x times power of x to n minus one, bottoming out at one when the exponent reaches zero; square the half-power to make it logarithmic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Raising a number x to an integer power n means multiplying x by itself n times. Recursively, the power of x to the n equals x multiplied by the power of x to the n minus one, with the base case that any number to the power zero is one. This naive recursion makes n calls and runs in linear time, while the fast-exponentiation variant that squares the result of the half power runs in logarithmic time by halving the exponent each step.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India computes how Rajesh's fixed deposit grows when a fixed growth factor is applied every year for several years. Applying the factor for five years is the factor multiplied by itself five times. The recursive idea is simple: growth over five years equals the factor times the growth over four years, and growth over zero years is just one, meaning no growth applied yet. Each step peels off one year until there are none left.

**One line to remember:** Power of x to n is x times power of x to n minus one, bottoming out at one when the exponent reaches zero; square the half-power to make it logarithmic.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive recursion follows the definition directly. The base case is that x to the power zero is one, which stops the recursion. The recursive case is that x to the power n equals x multiplied by x to the power n minus one. For example, two to the power three is two times two to the power two, which is two times two times two to the power one, which eventually bottoms out at two to the power zero equal to one, giving eight. This makes n multiplications and n stack frames, so it is linear in the exponent.

A much better approach is fast exponentiation, also called exponentiation by squaring. The insight is that x to the power n can be computed by halving the exponent: if n is even, x to the n equals the square of x to the n over two; if n is odd, x to the n equals x times the square of x to the n over two with integer division. This makes only about log n multiplications, which is dramatically faster for large exponents. For example two to the power ten computes two to the five, squares it, giving thirty-two squared equal to one thousand twenty-four, in far fewer steps than ten multiplications.

Negative exponents need handling. A negative exponent means the reciprocal, so x to the power negative n equals one divided by x to the power n. For integer results that becomes a fraction, so for banking I compute with a type that preserves precision rather than truncating. There is also a subtle pitfall: the most negative int cannot be negated safely because its magnitude exceeds the maximum positive int, so I promote to long before negating when handling that edge.

A senior point is overflow and precision. For integer bases and large exponents the result overflows a long very quickly, so for real financial growth factors I use BigDecimal, which has arbitrary precision and never silently overflows, and I set an explicit scale and rounding mode so the money math is exact and auditable. Using double for compounding money is a classic bug because of binary rounding, so I avoid it.

Another senior point is recursion depth. The naive version recurses n deep, which for a very large n could overflow the call stack; the logarithmic version only recurses about log n deep, so it is safe. In production I usually write the iterative squaring loop to avoid any stack concern entirely.

A small finance-domain example using the fast method conceptually: `BigDecimal power(BigDecimal x, int n) { if (n == 0) return BigDecimal.ONE; BigDecimal half = power(x, n / 2); BigDecimal sq = half.multiply(half); return (n % 2 == 0) ? sq : sq.multiply(x); }` computes a growth factor raised to n years in logarithmic steps.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers Rajesh a fixed deposit whose value grows by a fixed factor each year, and the statement must show the projected value after a chosen number of years. Projecting the value means raising the growth factor to the power of the number of years and multiplying by the principal. Computing that power is exactly this recursion.

This is exactly how recursive power works in Java — the projection for n years is the factor times the projection for n minus one years, bottoming out at one.

Problem 2 — The bank projects very long horizons, such as thirty or forty years, for retirement products, so the naive linear recursion is wasteful and risks deep recursion. The service must use fast exponentiation by squaring to compute the factor raised to a large power in logarithmic time, and it must use BigDecimal so the money math is precise and never overflows.

What the code will do: a `GrowthProjector` class with a `powerNaive(BigDecimal x, int n)` for teaching clarity and a `powerFast(BigDecimal x, int n)` using squaring, plus a `project(BigDecimal principal, BigDecimal factor, int years)` that multiplies principal by the factor raised to the years. The demo projects Rajesh's deposit over a short and a long horizon.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: principal is `1000000`, growth factor is `1.07`, and the horizon is `5` years.

Step 1: `project` calls `powerFast(1.07, 5)`. Since five is not zero, it recurses with five divided by two, which is two.

Step 2: `powerFast(1.07, 2)` recurses with two divided by two, which is one. `powerFast(1.07, 1)` recurses with one divided by two, which is zero.

Step 3: `powerFast(1.07, 0)` hits the base case and returns one. Back in the call for exponent one, half is one, squared is one, and because one is odd we multiply by x, giving `1.07`.

Step 4: Back in the call for exponent two, half is `1.07`, squared is `1.1449`, and because two is even we return `1.1449`. Back in the call for exponent five, half is `1.1449`, squared is about `1.31079601`, and because five is odd we multiply by `1.07`, giving about `1.4025517`.

Step 5: `project` multiplies the principal `1000000` by the grown factor about `1.4025517`, giving about `1402551.73`, and scales it to two decimal places with half-up rounding so the rupee amount is exact to the paise.

Step 6: For the thirty-year horizon the same squaring recursion runs, but only about five levels deep instead of thirty, computing the factor raised to thirty in logarithmic steps and projecting a much larger value. BigDecimal keeps every digit exact with no overflow.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T15:30:00Z INFO Projected value after 5 years = Rs.1402551.73
2026-10-26T15:30:00Z INFO Rajesh 5-year projection: Rs.1402551.73
2026-10-26T15:30:00Z INFO Projected value after 30 years = Rs.7612255.04
2026-10-26T15:30:00Z INFO Rajesh 30-year retirement projection: Rs.7612255.04
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: principal 1,000,000, factor 1.07, years 5
    │
    ▼
  powerFast(1.07, 5)  — squaring recursion
    │ n=5 → half=powerFast(1.07,2)
    │ n=2 → half=powerFast(1.07,1)
    │ n=1 → half=powerFast(1.07,0)=1 → square=1, odd → ×1.07 = 1.07
    │ n=2 → square(1.07)=1.1449 (even)
    │ n=5 → square(1.1449)=1.31.. odd → ×1.07 = 1.4025517
    ▼
  principal × 1.4025517 = 1,402,551.73 (scale 2, HALF_UP)
    │
    ├─ 30-year path: ~5 recursion levels (log n), BigDecimal exact
    ▼
  Output: projected FD values, precise to the paise
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Raising a number to an integer power recursively follows the definition directly: the power of x to the n is x times the power of x to the n minus one, with the base case that any number to the power zero is one. That naive version does n multiplications and recurses n deep, so it is linear in the exponent.

The improvement I always reach for is exponentiation by squaring. I compute the half power once, square it, and multiply by x one extra time when the exponent is odd. That turns n multiplications into about log n, which is a huge saving for large exponents, and it only recurses about log n deep, so there is no stack-overflow risk. I also handle negative exponents as the reciprocal, and I am careful with the most negative integer, which cannot be negated safely in int, so I promote to long first.

The senior point for banking is precision. For money I never use double because binary rounding corrupts compounding; I use BigDecimal, which has arbitrary precision and never silently overflows, and I set an explicit scale and rounding mode so the result is exact to the paise and auditable.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to project the future value of Rajesh's fixed deposit, raising the annual growth factor to the number of years and multiplying by the principal. For short horizons the clarity of the recursion is fine, but for thirty- or forty-year retirement projections I use the squaring version so it stays fast and shallow, all computed in BigDecimal. Explaining both the clean recursion and the logarithmic optimisation, plus the money-precision point, shows the interviewer that I understand recursion, complexity, and the real constraints of financial calculation.
